name: The two European philosophical traditions: British and Continental
plain_explanation: Russell divides post-Locke European philosophy into two families: a 'British' line (Locke, Berkeley, Hume, and later Mill) that reasons cautiously from many observed facts to modest conclusions, and a 'Continental' line (Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, and later Kant and Hegel) that builds large, systematic conclusions from a few very general logical principles.
precise_definition: The British method draws 'a comparatively modest conclusion ... from a broad survey of many facts,' with a stable, base-heavy structure that can absorb local errors without total collapse; the Continental method 'pyramids' a vast edifice of deduction upon 'a pin-point of logical principle,' producing an unstable structure that total collapse if any part of the foundation is flawed.
why_it_mattered: This methodological contrast, for Russell, explains much of the substantive divergence between the two traditions on metaphysics (acceptance vs. rejection of a priori proofs of God), ethics (pleasure vs. 'noble' anti-utilitarian ends), and even politics (piecemeal reform vs. sweeping revolutionary or reactionary programmes).
historical_origin: Traced by Russell from Locke and Hume on one side, Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz on the other, surviving (he argues) even Kant's attempted synthesis.
examples: Hume's inductive handling of the 'missing shade of blue' objection to his own principle, which he treats as non-fatal because his method is empirical, not logical
Leibniz's monadology, deduced from the premise that whatever is complex must be composed of simples, which cannot be extended, hence not material, hence mental
competing_positions: Kant's own belief that he had synthesized the two traditions, which Russell rejects as historically false, since Kant's followers remained squarely in the Cartesian tradition
influence_on_later_thinkers: Survives, per Russell, 'unvarying' from Descartes to Hegel on one side and from Locke to John Stuart Mill on the other, despite Kant's intervention.
